# What is visible, and to whom

What this tool can record depends on the account you are reading and the
account you are reading it as. **Every row below was measured, not assumed** -
by reading one account as a viewer and again while logged in as it.

| | Private, you follow it | Public, as a viewer | Logged in as the account |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Photographs, videos, captions, timestamps | yes | yes | yes |
| Post or reel, photo and video counts | yes | yes | yes |
| Comment counts | yes | yes | yes |
| **Like counts** | yes, but see below | **unreliable on older posts** | yes |
| **Follower names** | none - nothing to open | a partial sample | **complete** |
| Follower count | yes | yes | yes |
| **View counts** | no | no | **yes, for reels** |

## Like counts

Scanning one public account both ways, its four most recent posts reported the
same likes either way, while four older ones reported **3** likes to a viewer
and **41, 54, 34 and 28** to the account itself.

A low like count read as a viewer may be a placeholder rather than a number,
and there is no way to tell from the outside which it is.

::: {.callout-warning title="Treat a viewer's like count as a lower bound"}

It is never higher than the truth, and on older posts it can be far lower.

:::

## Follower names

Read as a viewer, the follower dialog is virtualised: five different
strategies each returned between **432 and 459** of one account's 603 names.
Logged in as the account, the same code returned **606** - Instagram serves
the list properly, and the tool reads it from those responses rather than from
the rendered rows.

So follower tracking is worth doing only for accounts you can log in as. For
anyone else's account you get a reliable count and a large sample of names.

A snapshot records the count it was aiming for and whether it matched, and
**two partial snapshots are never compared** - that would invent departures,
since a name missing from one run is usually a name that run did not see.

## View counts

Instagram leaves `view_count` null in every post's page data - for viewers and
for the account itself, and even on a reel with 627,728 likes. The number is
not in the data at all.

It is drawn on the tiles of the profile's **reels tab**, though, and that is
visible when the account is looking at its own profile.
[`scan`](commands.qmd#scan) reads it there in a single pass before walking the
posts, and records it against each reel.

A post that is not a reel has no count, and neither does any reel seen by
anyone but the account itself. Those stay blank rather than zero.
